strengths: The method offers a useful, modular extension to gradient-based multi-task learning: it separately aggregates loss and flatness components of task gradients. It works with four existing optimizers without changing the model architecture or inference procedure.

The empirical evaluation covers classification, 40 facial attributes, and dense scene understanding. Paired improvements are broadly consistent: F-CAGrad improves MultiFashion average accuracy from 86.51% to 87.82% and reduces CelebA average error from 8.52% to 8.22%. F-IMTL improves CityScapes segmentation mIoU from 75.33 to 76.63 while improving both depth metrics.

Table 5 provides direct evidence for the proposed aggregation design beyond simply adding task-wise SAM: on CityScapes, separate aggregation improves mIoU from 68.93 to 73.77 compared with direct aggregation.

The supplementary calibration results, gradient-conflict measurements, training curves, and radius sensitivity analysis provide useful supporting evidence. For example, MultiFashion average ECE decreases from 0.117 to 0.033. Pseudocode, architecture descriptions, training schedules, and attribution of underlying methods and datasets help readers understand the approach.
weaknesses: The theoretical motivation does not establish the behavior claimed for the actual update. Equation (4) bounds losses under joint shared/head perturbations, whereas Algorithm 1 evaluates each perturbed block with the other block unperturbed. Separately aggregating loss and flatness gradients and then adding them also need not preserve a common descent direction because cross-component conflicts can remain. The bound therefore motivates sharpness regularization but does not justify the superiority or simultaneous-descent properties of the proposed aggregation.

The supplementary proofs need correction. Theorem 3 changes failure probabilities to delta/2 without updating the displayed complexity terms; a simultaneous task guarantee requires appropriate confidence accounting. Theorem 4's Gaussian-tail correction omits the loss-bound factor L. Moreover, applicability of the bounded-loss assumption to the experimental objectives is not established. Some corrections appear repairable without changing the algorithm, but the guarantee is not demonstrated as written.

Evidence isolating the central novelty is limited to the MGDA/CityScapes comparison in Table 5. Most other experiments compare against optimizers without sharpness regularization, so they cannot distinguish benefits of separate aggregation from benefits of SAM/ASAM itself. Direct-aggregation comparisons for additional optimizers and datasets would materially strengthen the contribution.

Reproducibility and practical cost remain incompletely documented. Appendix C uses ASAM, while the main derivation and pseudocode describe ordinary Euclidean SAM; the implemented modification should be explicit. The manuscript reports extensive radius tuning but omits selected values and a clear selection protocol. Additional task-specific perturbed evaluations and two aggregation operations also warrant runtime and memory measurements, particularly for 40-task CelebA.

The evidence supports average improvements more strongly than coherent improvement of every task. On NYUv2, F-MGDA reduces segmentation mIoU from 30.47 to 26.42, an acknowledged but substantial tradeoff. Tables 2–4 omit variability estimates, limiting assessment of smaller gains. Claims concerning noisy-label and low-resource robustness also extend beyond the reported parameter-perturbation experiments.
